The targeted check in P1 verifies the equivalence for arbitrary rings and 2-regular modules, including the graph description, and credits **Hua, findings register, 67-involution-modules-triples** for the supplied finding. It does not verify Hua’s reported Lean code, which is absent from this context.

body: For “équivalence de catégories,” take a morphism of triples to be a pair \((f,g)\) whose reductions carry \(m\) into the target gluing submodule. This is the same missing convention explicitly supplied by Hua’s project, and P1 checks its naturality rather than treating object classification alone as categorical equivalence. Confidence is high because the inverse-image construction restricts \(f\oplus g\) functorially and the two multiplication-by-two identifications commute with every such map.

body: The uncertain retained assertion “\(P,Q\) inv. de rg \(1\)” does not follow from only commutativity, 2-regularity, rank-two projectivity and the global condition \(\sigma\ne\pm1\). With \(k=\mathbf Q\times\mathbf Q\), \(M=k^2\), and \(\sigma=(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1),1)\), the eigenspace ranks are \((1,2)\) and \((1,0)\), so they are not invertible; P2 gives the check. Confidence is high for this conditional literal reading, but the cancelled/obscured earlier hypotheses prevent treating it as a refutation of a definite fully legible final theorem.

Changing generators of the two eigenspaces changes the nonzero graph slope by the ratio of their reduced units, proving this refinement in P3. Confidence is high; Hua’s modernised reading retains surjectivity and therefore states a conditional two-class conclusion, whereas the frozen scan records its deletion.

body: A concrete test of “puis une” is \(k=\mathbf Z[(1+\sqrt{-11})/2]\): it is a norm-Euclidean PID, has residue field \(\mathbf F_4\) at 2, and its only units \(\pm1\) both reduce to 1. Thus E04 gives three nonsplit classes and one split class, so the two-class count requires the qualification. Confidence is high because P3 proves the Euclidean bound \(15/16<1\), identifies the unit and residue groups, and supplies exact involution matrices; the arithmetic script checks those matrices without claiming that a finite search proves conjugacy classification.

The index-two inclusion is compatible with the same conformal structure and reflection, so it induces a real isogeny from the split to the nonsplit torus. This supplies a concrete instance of the manuscript’s aside and of Hua’s corresponding assertion, without identifying the two real isomorphism types.

body: For “il y a deux orbites,” write the reflections of \(D_n\) as \(r^j\sigma\); rotation conjugacy changes \(j\) by an even number. Since \(n=2,4,6\), this gives exactly two classes, while the translation action of the rotation group on all reflections is free. P4 verifies the distinction between these two actions that the manuscript emphasizes and Hua restates.

body: The square gives both \(E_1\) and \(E'_1\) because the axis eigenvectors generate the lattice, whereas the diagonal eigenvectors \(e_0+e_1,e_0-e_1\) span an index-two sublattice. Thus the two real forms have different real-locus topology despite one underlying square complex torus. This makes concrete the point where scan95’s anticipated split/nonsplit dichotomy does hold, as Hua’s case distinction explains.

The two conjugations \(\sigma\) and \(-\sigma\) leave that complex curve fixed, so \(j(a)=j(1/a)\), whereas any nonzero constant multiple of \(\log a\) changes sign. Confidence is high for rejecting the suggested formula under that interpretation; Hua points instead to \(j(\tau)\), and the exact handwritten coefficient remains a separate doubt (E23).

body: The formula “\(H^1(\gamma,E(\mathbf C))\simeq\pi_+/(1+\sigma)\pi\)” follows from the exact sequence with \(V\) and the vanishing of positive-degree cohomology of a real vector space under a group of order two. In the split lattice the norm image is \(2\pi_+\), while in the nonsplit lattice \((1+\sigma)v=u\) fills \(\pi_+\), giving \(\mathbf Z/2\) and 0. P6 checks precisely the computation that Hua already explains; it is an abelian lattice calculation, not the unresolved nonabelian computation in the results register.

body: An explicit representative of \(E_a^!\) is the torus \(\mathbf C/(\mathbf Z+i\sqrt a\,\mathbf Z)\) with descent map \(z\mapsto\bar z+1/2\). Its square is a period translation and it has no fixed points, while its action on differences is the conjugation of \(E_a\), so it realizes the nonzero torsor class computed on the page. Confidence is high because these properties are direct calculations in P6; the construction adds a concrete model to Hua’s cohomological description without claiming novelty.
